nameStory: While this species doesn't have a widely-used common name, its scientific name 'aurantia' comes from the Latin word for orange or golden, likely referring to its coloration. Sea slugs like this one are called 'nudibranchs,' which literally means 'naked gills' because their breathing structures are exposed on the outside of their bodies rather than hidden inside a shell.
description: Tenellia aurantia is a tiny sea slug that belongs to a group called nudibranchs - soft-bodied marine creatures that look like underwater aliens. These delicate animals have finger-like projections called cerata covering their backs, which help them breathe and digest food. They're shell-less relatives of snails and slugs, perfectly adapted for life crawling along the ocean floor. Like other nudibranchs, they're typically quite small, usually measuring less than an inch long.

idTips.label: Body projections
idTips.description: Look for numerous finger-like cerata (say-RAH-ta) extending from the back - these soft, fleshy projections feel delicate and may have orange or golden coloration

idTips.label: Head tentacles
idTips.description: Two pairs of tentacles on the head - oral tentacles near the mouth and longer rhinophores that sense chemicals in the water

idTips.label: Soft body
idTips.description: Completely soft, squishy body with no shell - feels gelatinous to gentle touch and can contract when disturbed

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small creature, typically less than half an inch long - easy to overlook among seaweed and rocks

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Glides smoothly along surfaces using a muscular foot, leaving a barely visible slime trail like a terrestrial slug

habitat: Found in shallow marine waters along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools and areas with abundant hydroids (their preferred food). Look for them crawling on rocks, seaweed, or pier pilings in protected bays and coves. They prefer areas with good water circulation but protection from heavy wave action.

seasonality.spring: More active as water temperatures begin to warm, often found in shallow tide pools during low tide exploration.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be observed feeding and reproducing in warmer coastal waters.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to slightly deeper waters as temperatures begin to cool in late season.
seasonality.winter: Least active period, likely in deeper waters and rarely encountered by casual observers due to harsh conditions.

funFact: This tiny sea slug was actually mistaken for a different species for years until DNA testing revealed it was its own unique species - a reminder that even in our well-studied New England waters, there are still mysteries waiting to be solved!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small nudibranchs in tide pools, especially the closely related Tenellia viridis (Green Aeolis), but the orange-golden coloration of T. aurantia versus the greenish tones of its relative can help distinguish them.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name has changed over time - this species was formerly called Catriona aurantia before being reclassified into the genus Tenellia, showing how our understanding of relationships between species continues to evolve with new research techniques.
compareHints: Compared to the Green Aeolis (Tenellia viridis), this species shows more orange or golden coloration rather than green tones. Unlike the Naked Ear Aeolid (Tenellia gymnota), T. aurantia was proven to be a distinct species through DNA analysis despite their similar appearance. The orange coloration referenced in its scientific name is often the best field character for distinguishing it from its close relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its relatives the Naked Ear Aeolid which lacks the vibrant green color, or the Spotted Lagoon Aeolid which has distinctive spots, the Green Aeolis maintains its solid green coloration throughout its body and cerata.
Among its Tenellia relatives, the Naked Ear Aeolid is distinguished by its particularly translucent appearance and the arrangement of its cerata.
Unlike its relative the Green Aeolis which has a more uniform greenish coloration, the Spotted Lagoon Aeolid displays distinct dark spots on a translucent background.
Unlike the Green Aeolis which has a distinctly greenish coloration, Tenellia pustulata is more translucent with its characteristic bumpy texture.
